## Question 1: Compare KNN and logistic regression

Use [breast-cancer.csv](data/breast-cancer.csv), which contains 569 cases from the [Wisconsin Diagnostic Breast Cancer dataset](https://archive.ics.uci.edu/dataset/17/breast%2Bcancer%2Bwisconsin%2Bdiagnostic). Predict `y` (1 for malignant and 0 for benign) using `mean_radius`, `mean_texture`, and `mean_smoothness`.

Set a random seed and randomly split the observations into 70% training and 30% test data. Use the same split for every model. Standardize the predictors using the training means and standard deviations, and apply the same transformations to the test data.

```{python}
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsClassifier
from sklearn.metrics import roc_curve, roc_auc_score

data = pd.read_csv("data/breast-cancer.csv")

X = data[["mean_radius", "mean_texture", "mean_smoothness"]]
y = data["y"]

X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
    X,
    y,
    test_size=0.30,
    random_state=43206,
)

train_mean = X_train.mean()
train_sd = X_train.std()

X_train_std = (X_train - train_mean) / train_sd
X_test_std = (X_test - train_mean) / train_sd
```

Fit ordinary logistic regression with an intercept and no penalty, and KNN with Euclidean distance, equal neighbor weights, and

$$
k\in\{5,15,25,35,45\}.
$$

```{python}
logistic = LogisticRegression(
    C=np.inf,
    solver="lbfgs",
    tol=1e-10,
    max_iter=1000,
)

logistic.fit(X_train_std, y_train)

logistic_prob = logistic.predict_proba(X_test_std)[:, 1]
logistic_auc = roc_auc_score(y_test, logistic_prob)

k_values = [5, 15, 25, 35, 45]

knn_probs = {}
knn_aucs = {}

for k in k_values:
    knn = KNeighborsClassifier(
        n_neighbors=k,
        weights="uniform",
        p=2,
    )

    knn.fit(X_train_std, y_train)

    prob = knn.predict_proba(X_test_std)[:, 1]

    knn_probs[k] = prob
    knn_aucs[k] = roc_auc_score(y_test, prob)
```

Using the estimated probabilities for `y = 1` on the test data, plot all six ROC curves in one figure and report their AUC values. Which of the six fitted models do you prefer? Give a brief justification based on your results.

```{python}
plt.figure(figsize=(8, 8))

# Logistic regression
fpr, tpr, thresholds = roc_curve(y_test, logistic_prob)

plt.plot(
    fpr,
    tpr,
    linewidth=2,
    label=f"Logistic (AUC = {logistic_auc:.3f})",
)

# KNN models
for k in k_values:
    fpr, tpr, thresholds = roc_curve(y_test, knn_probs[k])

    plt.plot(
        fpr,
        tpr,
        linewidth=2,
        label=f"KNN k={k} (AUC = {knn_aucs[k]:.3f})",
    )

# Random-classifier reference line
plt.plot([0, 1], [0, 1], linestyle="--")

plt.xlabel("False-positive rate")
plt.ylabel("True-positive rate")
plt.title("Test ROC Curves")
plt.legend()
plt.show()

print(f"Logistic Regression: {logistic_auc:.3f}")

for k in k_values:
    print(f"KNN k={k}: {knn_aucs[k]:.3f}")
```

I would choose logistic regression because it had the highest test AUC. The KNN models also performed well, especially with larger values of k, but logistic regression did the best at separating malignant and benign cases on the test data. AUC measures how well the model ranks malignant cases above benign cases across different cutoffs. A larger AUC means better separation between the two classes.

## Question 2: Training and test ROC curves

Use the same data, training/test split, and standardization as in Question 1. Fit KNN with Euclidean distance, equal neighbor weights, and

$$
k\in\{1,3,5,10,20\}.
$$

Use each fitted model to estimate probabilities for both the training and test observations. For training predictions, include each observation itself among its $k$ nearest neighbors.

```{python}
k_values_q2 = [1, 3, 5, 10, 20]

train_aucs = {}
test_aucs = {}
train_probs = {}
test_probs = {}

for k in k_values_q2:
    knn = KNeighborsClassifier(
        n_neighbors=k,
        weights="uniform",
        p=2,
    )

    knn.fit(X_train_std, y_train)

    train_prob = knn.predict_proba(X_train_std)[:, 1]
    test_prob = knn.predict_proba(X_test_std)[:, 1]

    train_probs[k] = train_prob
    test_probs[k] = test_prob

    train_aucs[k] = roc_auc_score(y_train, train_prob)
    test_aucs[k] = roc_auc_score(y_test, test_prob)
```

For each $k$, use a separate panel to show the training and test ROC curves together. Report both AUC values.

```{python}
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 3, figsize=(15, 10))

axes = axes.flatten()

for ax, k in zip(axes, k_values_q2):
    # Training ROC
    train_fpr, train_tpr, _ = roc_curve(
        y_train,
        train_probs[k],
    )

    # Test ROC
    test_fpr, test_tpr, _ = roc_curve(
        y_test,
        test_probs[k],
    )

    ax.plot(
        train_fpr,
        train_tpr,
        linewidth=2,
        label=f"Train AUC = {train_aucs[k]:.3f}",
    )

    ax.plot(
        test_fpr,
        test_tpr,
        linewidth=2,
        label=f"Test AUC = {test_aucs[k]:.3f}",
    )

    ax.plot([0, 1], [0, 1], linestyle="--")

    ax.set_title(f"k = {k}")
    ax.set_xlabel("False-positive rate")
    ax.set_ylabel("True-positive rate")
    ax.legend()

# Turn off unused sixth panel
axes[-1].axis("off")

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

for k in k_values_q2:
    print(
        f"k={k}: "
        f"Train AUC={train_aucs[k]:.3f}, "
        f"Test AUC={test_aucs[k]:.3f}"
    )
```

Explain the difference between training and test performance and how it changes with $k$. In particular, explain what happens at $k=1$ and why training performance may not reflect performance on new observations.

When k = 1, each training observation is its own nearest neighbor. Because of this, the model gives every training observation its correct class probability, so the training AUC is 1. This does not mean the model will perform perfectly on new data. Training performance is better than test performance because the model was fit using the training data. Test performance gives a better idea of how the model will work on new observations. Small values of k make KNN very flexible and can lead to overfitting. As k increases, the model averages over more neighbors, which makes the predictions smoother and usually reduces overfitting. If k becomes too large, though, the model can become too smooth and lose useful patterns. Training AUC is highest for small values of k, especially k = 1, because the model fits the training data very closely. At k = 1, every training observation is its own nearest neighbor, so the training AUC is 1. However, test AUC is lower because new observations cannot use themselves as neighbors. As k increases, KNN becomes less flexible and less likely to overfit, so training and test performance become more similar.
